newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN war reparations fund to review Iraqi request.
newsitem.headline: UN war reparations fund to review Iraqi request.

text.p: Iraq's request for a greater voice in the U.N. body set up to compensate victims of the Gulf War will be reviewed by the 15 Security Council members on Friday in Geneva, diplomats and U.N. sources said on Thursday.
The closed-door meeting of the Governing Council of the United Nations Compensation Commission, composed of the same 15 member states as the Security Council, will be informal.
Diplomats will debate an official Iraqi request to be granted two hours to present Baghdad's case for fuller participation at the Governing Council's next formal session on October 14.

Western diplomats vowed to resist giving Baghdad an opportunity to make a frontal attack on the reparations fund set up by the Security Council in 1991 to assess claims for damages caused by Iraq's invasion of Kuwait.

"The purpose of Iraq's request is not reasonable. It is out of order and out of the question," a Western diplomat told Reuters. "We don't want them to dominate our agenda or our time with their pontificating.
"They want to make a broad-side attack on the Commission. At least four out of the five permanent members of the Security Council think they should be given just 15 minutes," he added.

Under traditional rules of procedure for non-Security Council member states, Iraq has been limited to making 15-minute presentations to the forum. However, it may file defence statements and attend oral hearings on various claims.
"They believe the whole concept of reparations, of verifying claims is incorrect," a U.N. source told Reuters.
"We have to review how the Council is going to proceed with the request. There is a wide variety of views on what Iraq should be allowed to speak on and for how long.

Another Western diplomat said: "We will consider Iraq's request for greater participation in the examination of claims against it. But there will be no talk of any political question beyond that, such as resolution 986."

The Security Council resolution, known as the oil-for-food deal, would have provided the cash-strapped Commission with $100 million a month over a six-month period, as it is to receive one-third of any Iraqi oil sale revenues.

But the plan, which would allow Iraq to enter the international oil markets for the first time in six years to sell $2 billion worth of crude to purchase food and other relief items, has been put on hold after Iraq's offensive in the north to aid a Kurdish faction, which prompted a U.S. missile attack.

The Geneva-based Commission, a subsidiary organ of the Security Council, has received more than 2.6 million claims against Iraq with an asserted total value of more than $200 billion, from individuals, corporations and governments.
It has approved $3.7 billion in claims to individuals who suffered serious injury or death of a close relative.
But financed in part by seized Iraqi assets as well as contributions from other countries, it has only been able to pay out some $13 million worth of these approved claims.
